title: From Teosinte to Maize
text:
Maize, one of the world's most important crops, looks very different from its wild ancestor. That ancestor, a grass called teosinte that still grows in southern Mexico, produces small ears containing only five to twelve kernels, each enclosed in a hard case that protects it from being digested by animals. A single maize cob, by contrast, can hold several hundred exposed kernels. For many years, the difference was so great that some botanists doubted that teosinte could be the ancestor at all.

Genetic studies have since settled the question. They show that maize was domesticated from teosinte roughly 9,000 years ago in the Balsas River valley of Mexico. Remarkably, many of the most visible changes are controlled by a small number of genes. A change in one gene, for instance, exposed the kernels by reducing the hard case around them, making the grain far easier to eat. Early farmers, by repeatedly planting seeds from the plants they preferred, gradually increased the frequency of such traits.

Domesticated maize also lost the ability to spread on its own. Because its kernels remain firmly attached to the cob and are wrapped in husks, the plant cannot scatter its seeds. Maize therefore depends entirely on human beings for its survival, a striking example of how domestication can create mutual dependence between people and the species they cultivate.

title: How Camels Survive in the Desert
text:
Camels are famous for surviving in some of the hottest and driest places on Earth. Many people believe that a camel stores water in its hump, but this is not true. The hump is made mostly of fat. By keeping its fat in one place instead of spreading it under the skin over the whole body, a camel can release heat more easily. The fat can also be broken down for energy when food is hard to find.

Camels have several ways of saving water. They produce very dry waste, and their kidneys make urine that is much more concentrated than human urine. A camel's body temperature can also rise by about six degrees Celsius during the day before it starts to sweat. This means that the animal loses less water through sweating. At night, its body cools down again.

When water is available, camels make up for lost time. A thirsty camel can drink more than 100 liters in about ten minutes. Most animals would become ill if they drank so much so quickly, but a camel's red blood cells have an unusual oval shape and can swell without bursting as water rushes into the blood. Thanks to these features, camels can travel long distances across the desert, which is why people have depended on them for thousands of years.

questions.explanation: Each paragraph describes features that allow camels to live in hot, dry places.

title: Critical Periods in the Developing Brain
text:
During certain windows of early development, the brain is unusually receptive to particular kinds of experience. These intervals, known as critical periods, were first demonstrated convincingly in studies of vision. When one eye of a young mammal was temporarily deprived of patterned light, neurons in the visual cortex that would normally respond to that eye were taken over by connections from the other eye, and the deprived eye remained functionally impaired even after normal input was restored. The same deprivation imposed on an adult animal produced little lasting effect.

Such findings encouraged a view of the developing brain as a structure that is shaped by experience and then, to a considerable extent, fixed. The closure of a critical period is now understood to be an active process rather than a passive loss of capacity. As circuits mature, inhibitory neurons strengthen, and molecular structures accumulate around certain cells, stabilizing existing connections and restricting the formation of new ones. Plasticity, in other words, is not simply exhausted; it is deliberately constrained.

This reconceptualization has notable implications. If the brakes on plasticity are imposed by identifiable mechanisms, it may be possible to loosen them. In experiments with rodents, treatments that reduce inhibition or dissolve the stabilizing structures have partially restored juvenile-like plasticity in adulthood, allowing recovery from early visual deprivation. Whether comparable interventions can be applied safely in humans remains uncertain, since the same constraints that limit plasticity presumably also protect established skills and memories.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Adult brains are as adaptable as the brains of young animals.
Treatments for early visual deprivation have been proven safe in humans.
Vision is the only ability that has a critical period.
Critical periods close through active mechanisms, which suggests that plasticity might be partly restored.
optionNotes: Contradicted: the same deprivation affected young animals but not adults.
Contradicted: whether such interventions are safe in humans remains uncertain.
Not stated: vision is where critical periods were first demonstrated, not the only case.
Correct: the passage moves from the discovery of critical periods to the active view of their closure and its implications.
questions.explanation: The central idea is the reinterpretation of closure as an active process, which opens the possibility of loosening it.
questions.evidence: The closure of a critical period is now understood to be an active process rather than a passive loss of capacity.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention that the same deprivation in an adult animal "produced little lasting effect"?

To show that the deprivation experiments were badly designed

optionNotes: Correct: the contrast with adults shows the effect depends on a developmental window, the defining feature of a critical period.
Not suggested: the experiments are described as convincing.
Not argued: the sentence concerns vulnerability to deprivation, not improvement.
Inhibitory neurons are discussed only in paragraph 2.
questions.explanation: A critical period is a window; comparing young and adult animals shows that the deprivation matters only during that window.
questions.evidence: The same deprivation imposed on an adult animal produced little lasting effect.

title: The Aqueducts of Rome
text:
At its height, ancient Rome was supplied by eleven aqueducts that together delivered an enormous volume of water to the city each day. This water supported public fountains, the private homes of the wealthy, and the large public baths that were central to Roman social life. Remarkably, the system used no pumps. It relied entirely on gravity, carrying water from springs in the hills along channels that descended very gradually toward the city.

Maintaining a steady downward slope over long distances was the engineers' central challenge. If the slope was too steep, fast-moving water would erode the channel; if it was too shallow, the water would stagnate. Surveyors used simple leveling instruments to plan routes that often followed the natural contours of the land. Contrary to popular images, most of an aqueduct's length ran underground in covered channels, which protected the water from contamination and evaporation. The famous arched bridges were built only where a route had to cross a valley.

Roman aqueducts required constant upkeep. Minerals in the water left hard deposits that gradually narrowed the channels, and workers had to chip them away. A permanent staff was employed to inspect the system, repair leaks, and prevent people from illegally tapping the supply. Several aqueducts remained in use for centuries, and one of them, after restoration, still feeds fountains in Rome today.

optionNotes: Contradicted: bridges were built only where routes crossed valleys; most channels were underground.
Contradicted: the system used no pumps.
Correct: the passage covers the gravity system, the challenge of the slope, and the upkeep.
Not stated: the baths are one of several uses, and no proportions are given.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces the gravity-based system, paragraph 2 the engineering challenge, and paragraph 3 the maintenance.
questions.evidence: It relied entirely on gravity, carrying water from springs in the hills along channels that descended very gradually toward the city.

title: How Plants Spread Their Seeds
text:
Plants cannot move from place to place, but their seeds can. If all of a plant's seeds simply fell beneath it, the young plants would have to compete with their parent and with one another for light, water, and nutrients. For this reason, many plants have developed ways to carry their seeds away.

Wind is one common method. The seeds of dandelions have tiny parachutes of soft hairs that allow them to float through the air, sometimes for several kilometers. Maple seeds have a flat wing that makes them spin as they fall, which slows them down so that the wind can push them farther from the tree.

Animals also help. Many plants produce sweet, colorful fruits. When a bird eats the fruit, the seeds pass through its body unharmed and are dropped in a new place, often with a little natural fertilizer. Other seeds have small hooks that catch on the fur of passing animals. An animal may carry these seeds a long way before they fall off or are brushed away. Finally, some plants, such as coconut palms, which often grow near beaches, use water. Their large seeds can float in the ocean for weeks and then begin to grow on a distant shore.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 explains why plants spread seeds; paragraphs 2 and 3 describe wind, animals and water.

title: Hidden Information in Markets
text:
Standard models of competitive markets assume that buyers and sellers are equally well informed about what is being traded. In many real transactions, however, one party knows considerably more than the other. A person selling a used car is far better placed than a prospective buyer to know whether the vehicle has hidden defects. Economists refer to such situations as markets with asymmetric information, and their analysis has shown that the imbalance can do more than disadvantage the less informed party: it can undermine the market itself.

Suppose buyers cannot distinguish good cars from defective ones and are therefore willing to pay only a price reflecting average quality. Owners of good cars, who know their vehicles are worth more than this average, will be reluctant to sell. As they withdraw, the average quality of cars on offer falls, buyers lower the price they will pay, and still more owners of good cars exit. In extreme cases, the process continues until only the worst products remain, and transactions that would have benefited both sides never take place.

Markets have developed numerous institutions that mitigate this problem. Warranties allow sellers of reliable goods to demonstrate their confidence, since a warranty on a defective product would be costly to honor. Independent inspections, brand reputations, and mandatory disclosure laws similarly narrow the information gap. The persistence of such mechanisms is itself evidence of how damaging unchecked asymmetries can be.

optionNotes: Correct: the passage defines asymmetric information, shows how it can destroy a market, and describes the remedies.

Contradicted: inspections, reputations and disclosure laws are also mentioned.
Opposite: in the example, the seller is better informed.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 introduces the concept and its danger, paragraph 2 explains the mechanism, and paragraph 3 describes the institutions that limit it.
questions.evidence: it can undermine the market itself
